title: can new generation hydropower dams save energy transition  ecmii 2026 03 27
text:
March 25 - Last year, despite the growing global demand for energy, countries began to report record levels of energy-dumping, or curtailment, which kicks in when electricity grids can no longer cope with the renewable energy being created.
In Brazil, for instance, 20% of the country’s solar power was reported to have been dumped last year, while collectively Germany, France and the Netherlands were forced to cut 3.9 terawatt hours (TWh) of renewable production. It’s a paradox that is vexing grid managers, as they search for ways to store this green energy rather than waste it.
“The record levels of curtailment we saw in 2025 are a clear warning ​sign,” says Eddie Rich, chief executive of the International Hydropower Association (IHA). “The world is building clean generation at a rapid rate … but now that rate must be matched by building the infrastructure needed to use it or to store it.”
When it comes to energy ‌storage, there is already a clear leader. There is nearly 200 GW of pumped storage hydro (PSH) capacity, accounting for 90% of long-duration energy storage globally. And preliminary figures from the IHA, ahead of its 2026 World Hydropower Outlook, show that another 570 gigawatts (GW) of PSH is being developed worldwide.
Around 40% of this is in China, which is already the global frontrunner, with over 50 GW of installed capacity. This includes the Fengning Pumped Storage Power Station, the largest facility of its kind in the world. Operated by the State Grid Corporation of China (SGCC), it has a total installed capacity of 3.6 GW. In comparison, Europe’s largest PSH plant, La Muela II, near Valencia, has a capacity of 850 megawatts (MW).
While lithium-ion batteries are the go-to solution ​to help manage daily peaks, long-duration energy storage (LDES) is needed for anything longer than four hours.
Conventional hydropower, such as the Three Gorges Dam, stores energy by holding water in a reservoir before releasing it to drive turbines. PSH – dubbed the world’s “water battery” – takes the technology further. It uses ​excess energy, most of it from renewables, to pump water from a lower reservoir to a higher one, before allowing gravity to take over, sending the water back down pipes to generate power. This helps to balance the ⁠grid and provide electricity in times of low production.
“It's proven, it's a reliable technology, it reduces greenhouse gas emissions (and) dependence on fossil fuel,” says Erik Steimle, chief development officer at U.S. hydropower developers Rye Development.
Pumped storage also helps safeguard the grid against blackouts and extreme weather events, he continues.
Figures from the U.S. ​Energy Information Administration (EIA) predict a 1% rise in energy demand this year and 3% growth in 2027, marking the strongest period of growth since the turn of the century.
Steimle says this is due to the growth in data centres, the need for more cooling such as air conditioning and a steady uptake in electric ​vehicles. “There's an urgent need for more electricity in the United States,” he says. “Pump storage is one of the ways to meet that growing demand while maintaining the stability of the grid.”
While established hydro energy players like EDF, Germany’s Voith Hydro and Enel are increasing investments in pumped storage, there are significant barriers to new entrants, including extensive construction costs, which require upfront investments ranging from $1,500-$2,500 per kilowatt hour, according to Intel Market Research.
Projects also face stringent environmental regulations, with 60% of proposed sites found unviable for ecological reasons or because of local opposition, its research finds.
The greatest growth is expected to come from innovative closed-loop pumped hydro designs, which avoid impacts on natural water bodies by pumping water between artificially constructed reservoirs.
One ​of the biggest proponents of closed-loop projects in the U.S. is Rye Development, a partnership between energy storage companies Climate Adaptive Infrastructure and EDF power solutions.
Rye is developing four closed-loop sites across the U.S. with Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP), the world’s largest investment fund focused on investments in greenfield energy.
In January, Rye ​received the go ahead to start building the Goldendale Energy Storage Project, on a ridge above the Columbia River in Washington State, with CIP covering the estimated $2-3 billion bill for construction.
“These projects don’t impact river ecosystems,” says Steimle. “The water is recycled over and over again.”
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission issued the plant with a 40-year licence, recognising its ‌potential to store ⁠electricity for up to 12 hours, and generate 1,200 MW of on-demand electricity, enough to power about 500,000 homes.
FERC rules say that work must start within two years of a licence being granted, and Rye will be hoping that more states follow California, which has mandated that power providers buy long-duration storage to balance the state’s huge supply of solar power. California already has 13 GW of grid-scale battery storage.
In the U.S., more than 90 projects are now being planned, but it will be at least a decade before the turbines are fired up, with developers first needing to find utilities that are prepared to commit to long-term deals to buy the energy.
The UK is also moving to take advantage of PHS, with plans to build 10 GW of capacity to support renewable energy integration by the mid 2030s.
Close to Inverness in the Scottish Highlands, the Earba Storage Project, developed by Gilkes Energy Ltd, will be the largest, with an installed capacity of up ​to 1,800 MW. Construction is due to start in 2028, with the project ​using Loch Leamhain as the upper reservoir and Loch Earba as ⁠the lower, connected by a 3km long tunnel. Close by, energy company SSE Renewables is investing 2 billion pounds in Coire Glas, which has a potential capacity of up to 1,300 MW.
These new developments are being built close to wind farms so that they are well placed to absorb surplus energy and then quickly and efficiently send it to where it’s most needed, explains William Gallimore, policy and advocacy lead at the British Hydropower Association (BHA).
“When we're looking at the transition to ​net zero, pump storage hydro power has taken quite a central role,” he says, especially as an alternative to expensive “peaking gas”, which kicks in when demand is high.
In the UK, the Department for Net Zero and Energy ​Security (DESNZ) is set to introduce a cap and ⁠floor mechanism that regulates revenue levels for PHS projects. It offers security to investors by protecting them from price volatility, while also setting a maximum price level, above which excess returns are given back to consumers.
“The problem is the market won't deliver it alone,” says Rich of IHA. “It’s difficult for investors to go into this unless they get… market signals set by the government.”
The other barrier developers face is red tape and what Rich of IHA calls “permitting paralysis”. He says licensing processes should be streamlined so projects that could be built in three years don’t end up taking 10.
The state-run Chinese system is much quicker, he says, with a centralised system that drives developments ⁠forward, construction teams that ​are used to large-scale infrastructure projects and supply chains that are geared up to meet these needs.
But speeding things up doesn’t mean cutting corners, he adds, and companies, including those in ​China, still need to adhere to the Hydropower Sustainability Standard, an independent global framework that has set out to create a more responsible and equitable energy sector.
Steimle says Rye first applied for a licence to develop Goldendale in 2020. Part of the problem, he says, is that the process is governed by laws written in the 1980s, the last time major infrastructure projects were undertaken.
But ​unlike other forms of renewable energy, PHS has bi-partisan support, including from within the White House, so there are efforts both inside FERC and federal government to reform the permitting process.
“If we are serious about energy security, energy sovereignty and resilience, pumped storage must be treated as the backbone, not an afterthought," says Rich.
